summary: This informational document discusses how to evaluate Information-Centric Networking and what its effects on network security might be. It surveys the tools currently available to researchers working on ICN and offers suggestions about methodology and metrics.

eli5.summary: Before building a new kind of road system, you must test it and think about the thieves. This explains how to test a network that finds data by name, and what new dangers it brings.

subtitle: Testing and securing a name-based networking approach

tldr.problem: Information-Centric Networking (ICN) is a fundamentally different approach to routing where packets request named content rather than reaching host addresses, but researchers lack common evaluation methodology and metrics, and ICN's security properties differ significantly from traditional TCP/IP networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys evaluation techniques including topology selection, traffic load modeling with Zipfian popularity distributions, and standard metrics (throughput, cache hit ratio, delay). It also analyzes ICN security changes: content authentication is addressed but authorization, privacy, and caching risks are not fully solved, and threat models differ from IP networks.
tldr.outcome: Researchers now have evaluation guidelines, metrics frameworks, and tools (simulators like ndnSIM, testbeds like POINT) to compare ICN approaches consistently, and operators understand the security trade-offs—especially privacy loss from in-network caching—that deployment would entail.

today: RFC 7945 is an Informational RFC published in September 2016 by the IRTF Information-Centric Networking Research Group. It has not been obsoleted. The evaluation framework and tools survey remain active; the ICNRG continues to refine metrics and add new tools to the public list. The security considerations have proven prescient: years later, ICN deployment discussions still emphasize that authorization, access control, and privacy mechanisms remain open problems, making RFC 7945 a foundational reference for understanding ICN's readiness level.

sections.title: From Host-Centric to Information-Centric Networking
sections.content: Traditional TCP/IP networks are host-centric: data flows from one host to another, and applications care about connecting to specific servers. Information-Centric Networking (ICN) flips this: applications request named content, and the network delivers it from any available source (a cache, a nearby server, or the original publisher). ICN appeals to researchers because it aligns with how people actually use the internet—searching for information, not tracking host locations. Different ICN architectures exist: CCN/NDN (Named Data Networking), NetInf, PURSUIT, COMET, and others. However, comparing these approaches is difficult because researchers use different topologies, traffic patterns, and metrics. This document, produced by the IRTF Information-Centric Networking Research Group, provides common evaluation guidelines, methodology, and an inventory of available tools so researchers can compare ICN proposals fairly and measure their improvements over IP networking.
sections.eli5: Old networks ask 'who has the data?'; new ones ask 'what data do you want?' This is a guide for testing which approach works better and what could go wrong.

sections.title: Evaluating ICN: Topology, Traffic, and Metrics
sections.content: Proper evaluation requires three components. Topology Selection: no single topology fits all studies. For scalability, use synthetic topologies (Barabasi-Albert or Watts-Strogatz). For cost studies, use realistic topologies inferred from Internet traces (CAIDA, Rocketfuel). For mobility, use Delay-Tolerant Networking topologies. Nodes must have defined storage, computation, and link capacity matrices. Traffic Load: content popularity follows a power law (often Zipfian with exponent 0.64 to 0.84 for web traffic). The RFC provides content catalogs for Web (10^12 items, 1-10 KB chunks), file sharing (5x10^6 items, 250-4096 KB chunks), user-generated content (10^8 items, ~10 MB objects), and video on demand (10^4 items, 100 MB objects or 1-5 KB segments with adaptive streaming). Metrics: traffic metrics (download time, goodput, startup latency, throughput, packet delay) measure user experience; system metrics (cache hit ratio, router energy, cost savings) measure efficiency. The RFC recommends using IPPM (IP Performance Metrics) framework where possible to enable comparison with IP networks.
sections.eli5: Test on realistic topologies, realistic traffic patterns (popular items are requested much more), and measure what matters: user speed and network resource use.

sections.title: ICN Security Challenges and Trade-Offs
sections.content: ICN architectures concentrate on content authentication—ensuring received data is genuine and uncorrupted—using cryptography to tie content names to content. However, three critical security gaps remain. Authorization and Access Control: once content is cached in routers or edge devices not controlled by the publisher, the publisher cannot enforce access control or revoke access. Encrypting content avoids this but requires out-of-band key distribution and negates caching benefits. Proposed solutions include delegation schemes and attribute-based encryption, but implementations are immature. Privacy: caching trades efficiency for privacy. First-hop routers see who requests what; while requests aggregate at subsequent hops, cache owners gain visibility into user behavior across time, potentially exposing sensitive access patterns. Threat Model Changes: ICN introduces new attack surfaces. Routers become powerful caches, attractive targets for attacks. Denial-of-service attacks may be harder (requests spread across caches) or easier (attackers can use caches as storage or craft requests that always miss). Lack of per-request authentication makes identifying attack sources difficult. These differences mean ICN deployment requires solving authorization, privacy, and access logging—problems IP networks solved years ago but that ICN leaves open.
sections.eli5: The new network finds content securely but doesn't stop people from caching secrets they shouldn't have, doesn't hide who asked for what, and opens new ways to attack routers.

sections.title: Evaluation Tools and Testbeds
sections.content: The RFC surveys three categories of tools. Open-Source Implementations include NDN (full protocol stack for deployment), CCN-lite (lightweight C implementation, ~1000 lines, ideal for courses), Blackadder (PURSUIT publish-subscribe for Linux and Android), and NetInf prototypes (Java caching proxy, HTTP/UDP convergence layer). Simulators enable large-scale experiments: ndnSIM (NDN module for ns-3, supports routing and caching strategies), ccnSim (CCN-specific for OMNeT++), and Icarus (Python-based, agnostic to architecture, with caching strategies like ProbCache and hash-route caching). Testbeds provide real experiments. The Open Network Lab (ONL) hosts 18 gigabit routers and 100+ client/server nodes running CCNx. The POINT testbed spans Europe, North America, and Japan with Blackadder. CUTEi (Container-Based ICN Testbed) uses Linux containers for isolation and supports both application-level and network-level experiments. An updated list is maintained at the ICNRG Wiki.
sections.eli5: Researchers can download code, run it in a simulator on their laptop, or book time on a real testbed with hundreds of machines.

sections.title: Comparative Evaluation and Resource Equivalence
sections.content: Comparing ICN to IP and comparing different ICN approaches requires care. IP performance is well-studied; ICN performance varies with architecture, content popularity, and cache capacity. A key challenge is resource equivalence: should you provision more link bandwidth or more cache memory? Different resources affect performance differently. Cache hit ratios, for instance, depend on cache size and request patterns. The RFC proposes using formulas like pi = [mu / (mu + lambda)]^N, where lambda is the request rate for desired content, mu is the request rate for other content moving it down the cache, and N is cache size, to estimate probability that content is cached. This quantifies cache benefit and can be compared against the gain from adding bandwidth. However, no consensus metric yet exists for directly trading off bandwidth against cache—an open research question.
sections.eli5: Is it better to add faster links or bigger storage? The RFC helps you measure both so you can choose.
